source.title: Fatigue, sleep loss, and confidence in judgment

confidence_rationale: Larger, better-powered replication of the same author's 1994 finding (also in this directory), across three tasks spanning different cognitive abilities. Same conclusion: traditional confidence-accuracy indices (calibration, resolution, over/underconfidence) remain stable across 28h of sleep deprivation. Held at 0.72, slightly above the 1994 entry, for the larger N, the broader task battery, and the higher-tier venue (APA journal) -- but capped short of 0.8 because it is still one research group's paradigm, not an independent replication.
failure_signatures: Across THREE different tasks (perceptual comparison, general knowledge, mental addition) spanning a range of cognitive demands and SD-susceptibility, over- and underconfidence indices and the accuracy of pre/post-task performance estimates all remained stable across 28 hours of sleep deprivation -- a within-study replication of the null found in the author's own 1994 study, now across a wider construct space.

The paper's own stated implication is that people can accurately assess their cognitive performance after one night without sleep, and that this self-assessment ability does not depend on subjective sleepiness ratings -- directly at odds with a picture in which waking confidence reliably and substantially inflates over a single wake episode.

mapping.source_claim_statement: In a 28-hour sleep deprivation study spanning perceptual comparison, general-knowledge, and mental-addition tasks, subjective and objective sleepiness measures showed the expected increase in fatigue, yet the confidence-accuracy relationship (calibration, resolution, over/underconfidence) and pre/post-task performance estimate accuracy remained stable throughout.
mapping.ree_translation: This strengthens the 1994 finding's weight against SD-076's premised drift by extending the null across three distinct task types rather than one, and by using a larger, more heterogeneous sample. For the GOV-FANOUT-1 H3 question specifically, it further supports reading V3-EXQ-794a's small, sub-threshold effect as plausibly close to (or even larger than) what the best-controlled human calibration literature would lead one to expect, rather than as evidence the mechanism form itself is wrong.
mapping.mapping_caveat: Same limitation as the companion 1994 entry: this is a total/partial sleep-loss study, not a REM-manipulation study, so it cannot directly test whether REM sleep specifically is the corrective process MECH-204 claims. It also measures confidence in performance on cognitive tasks generally, not an RL agent's continuously-updated running-variance estimate -- the update rule and its asymmetry are REE inventions with no direct human analogue tested here.
mapping.source_context: 64 healthy adult humans, 28 hours of continuous wakefulness and cognitive work, three tasks (perceptual comparison, general knowledge, mental addition), laboratory setting.

confidence_components.notes: Source quality above the 1994 companion entry: larger N (64 vs 16), three tasks instead of one, published in a higher-tier APA journal. Mapping fidelity and transfer risk unchanged from the companion entry, since it is the same construct (self-accuracy confidence) and the same domain gap to REE's running-variance estimate.
